facts.text: Gloster grew from a whistle stop named after a railroad engineer, marking the shift from isolated farms to a connected community.
Pine forests dominate Gloster’s uplands, while the nearby Red River alluvial plains provide fertile soils that support both timber and crop production.
The Greek‑Revival Thomas Scott House, built in 1858, sits just outside Gloster and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
After the Civil War, a timber boom fueled by housing demand and reforestation projects helped Gloster grow as logging operations expanded.
Gloster sits at 32°11′31″N 93°48′41″W, rising 243 feet above sea level in northwestern Louisiana.
From May through September, Gloster’s humidity climbs, with daytime highs often reaching the upper 90s Fahrenheit.
